newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks plunge to 8-year low on baht jitters.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks plunge to 8-year low on baht jitters.

text.p: Thai markets took a beating on Wednesday as investors took flight from the baht and drove the bourse to near eight-year lows on fears over the economy, a possible devaluation and uncertainty over economic portfolios.
The already-bearish market plunged 4.82 percent to close at 571.30 points on 6.5 billion baht ($250 million) turnover. The close was the lowest ending level since June 1989.
Foreign investors dumped shares across the board with bank, finance and communication sectors facing the heaviest onslaught.
"Foreigners were selling shares across the board. They were very worried about the economy and the baht selloff in the foreign exchange market," said one broker at a local brokerage.
Despite repeated assurances from the Bank of Thailand, the central bank, that it had no plans to change the currency system, investors were not convinced.

Analysts said investors did not think Thailand could allow lower interest rates to boost the sagging economy -- projected to grow at a decade-low of less than six percent this year -- without letting go of the baht.

Although devaluation could boost some exports as it makes Thai products cheaper abroad, the benefit would likely be clouded by a massive short-term negative impact, said Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Investors were jittery... because any baht devaluation now could send some companies into bankruptcy as they will have difficulties meeting debt obligations," she said.
"Thailand's foreign debt now stands around $90 billion and about 40 percent of that is short-term," she said.
However, analysts believed the Bank of Thailand would not devalue the baht and if there was any devaluation, it would be forced from outside.
The Bank of Thailand said in the afternoon it and the Monetary Authority of Singapore jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht.

The central bank said its action was "aimed at stemming excessive speculative activities which may lead to disorderly conditions in the Thai and regional financial markets". It said other appropriate measures would be taken as necessary.
The intervention helped the currency recover to 26.030-26.080 shortly after lunch. It weakened for a while in late trade before firming to about 25.950/26.050 by 1130 GMT.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, said political uncertainties exacerbated the baht worries and consequently the stock market.
There has been a persistent rumour since last week that Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan might step down, with some colleagues in the coalition government complaining about his performance.
But Amnuay told Reuters in Tokyo on Wednesday that he was confident in his future as finance minister.
"These uncertainties on whether Amnuay is really in charge do strongly affect the market," Song said.
"If one can bring stability to the political front... with Amnuay saying 'look I'm still in charge,' I think the pressure on the baht will lessen," he said.

Weak exports, poor first-quarter results, beleaguered property and finance sectors, and uncertainty over the scope of the government's effort to improve the situation have also been blamed for the stock market's recent falls. ($1 = 26 baht)
